description: We are a team from Jakarta taking on Challenge 6. Our project, SBATS (Space Base Analog Terrain System), compares about 92,000 land squares across Earth with real Moon and Mars sites using NASA and partner data. Pick a site, and SBATS shows where on Earth matches it, why, and what Earth cannot copy. We also test Indonesian volcanoes like Tambora and Batur as new analog candidates. Team: Prabu, Eliana, Mubashir, Eibee.
summary:
SBATS is a web tool that finds places on Earth that can stand in for future Moon and Mars base sites. Pick a real target, such as Shackleton Crater or Jezero Crater, and SBATS scores about 92,000 land squares across Earth against it using NASA and partner data on terrain, climate, rock type and ground cover. For every match it shows which factors agree, which do not, and what Earth cannot copy at all.

The challenge asks for new analogs, not the famous ones. SBATS searches the whole planet instead of starting from known sites, then checks itself: known analog sites score higher than 72% of all land squares. We also tested sites near home. Mount Tambora in Indonesia has crater walls nearly as steep as Shackleton Crater's, at about one third of its size, and the same rock class as Jezero Crater and the Marius Hills. We propose it as a practice site for steep-terrain and rock work, while being clear its tropical climate does not match.

This matters because every instrument, rover and crew procedure has to be tested on Earth first, and choosing the right test site saves missions time and money.
details:
What it does

SBATS searches all of Earth for places that can stand in for a Moon or Mars base site. You pick a real target, such as Shackleton rim or Gale crater, and the tool scores 91,894 land squares against it on terrain, bare ground, dryness, temperature, sunlight and rock type. You can also set your own conditions.

How it works

Each factor is compared with a similarity curve, and the factors are combined so that one complete mismatch cannot be hidden by the others. Terrain is measured the same way on all three worlds: Copernicus elevation on Earth, LRO LOLA on the Moon, MGS MOLA on Mars. The weights were fixed before testing. Known analog sites score higher than 72% of all land squares, and the Validation page also shows where the method is weak, such as for the Moon.

What you get

Every match is shown factor by factor, with both values, the source of each number, and what Earth cannot copy (gravity, vacuum, radiation). A match can be opened as 3D terrain with a rover route planned over real elevation, checked against what it could be used to test (landing, navigation, mobility, construction and more), explored against every other square on Earth, and exported as a cited report.

What is new

Our team proposed five sites, including Mount Tambora and Mount Batur in Indonesia, and the tool tested them. Tambora's crater walls are nearly as steep as Shackleton's and its rock class matches Jezero and the Marius Hills, at about a third of Shackleton's size. Its climate does not match, and the tool says so.

Benefits

Mission teams must test hardware and procedures on Earth first. SBATS helps choose where, shows what a site is good for, and is honest about where each comparison breaks down.

Tools

React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind and three.js for the app, and Python for the data pipeline. It is a static site with no server. Code was written with AI assistance (Claude Code) under the team's direction; details are in AI_USE.md in the repository: https://github.com/OrabuGit/sbats

The demo video's music was generated in code with AI assistance, and the video was edited with AI assistance.
